caseStudy.title: Delivered right first time: receiver confirmation
caseStudy.summary: Southern Cross Freight is a fictional national parcel carrier moving around 38,000 consignments a day through 14 depots. Only 79% of consignments arrive within their promised window and 9% fail at the first delivery attempt. The product team's goal is on-time last-mile delivery of 92% or better. Throughout the day we take the top backlog item — receiver delivery-window confirmation — from a feature to a story the team can build, verify and measure.
caseStudy.disclaimer: Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.

days.title: The Delivery Horizon — building the right things, correctly

blocks.title: The Agile Business Analyst at this horizon
Time frame · context, feedback and learning
Exercise: elaborate one backlog item · close

participant.bigIdea: The Delivery Horizon is where the right things get built correctly — in days, not months.
participant.overview:
Analysis at the Delivery Horizon ensures that **the right things are built correctly**. The question here is how each backlog item should be understood, elaborated and verified. This is where a product vision becomes tangible: working software, validated business rules and real user experiences.

Today follows the structure of the Delivery Horizon chapter of *Agile Business Analysis: A Guide to Product Thinking and Delivery*: the analyst's role, outcomes of analysis, time frame, context and feedback, the nine principles, then analysis techniques and planning and delivery techniques. You'll finish with one backlog item fully elaborated.

![The delivery iteration cycle](/visuals/horizons-delivery/delivery-cycle.svg)
objectives: Explain the purpose of analysis at the Delivery Horizon.
Describe the iteration cycle and where analysis happens in it.
Choose the backlog item you'll elaborate today.

keyPoints.title: Purpose
keyPoints.body: Ensure the right things are built correctly.

keyPoints.title: Continuous
keyPoints.body: Analysis is embedded in the rhythm of iterative delivery, not done up front.

keyPoints.title: Collaborative
keyPoints.body: Shared understanding is built through conversation, then captured.

sections.heading: The running case
sections.body:
**Southern Cross Freight** (fictional) moves about 38,000 consignments a day through 14 depots. Only 79% arrive within their promised window and 9% fail at the first delivery attempt. The product team's goal is on-time last-mile delivery of 92% or better.

The top item on the product backlog is **receiver delivery-window confirmation**: the evening before delivery, the receiver is asked to confirm they'll be in, or choose a safe drop, before routes lock at 5 am. Today we take that item from a feature on the backlog to a story the team can build and verify.

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

activities.title: Choose your backlog item
activities.instructions: Write down a backlog item from your own work that's coming up soon (or adopt 'receiver delivery-window confirmation'). Note who it's for and the value it should create.

participant.aiPrompt: I'm a business analyst preparing a backlog item for delivery. From the item and context below, summarise in five bullets what the delivery team needs to understand before work begins: the user, their context, the behaviour the product should exhibit, how success will be judged, and open questions. Item and context:

quiz.q: The purpose of analysis at the Delivery Horizon is to…
opts: Ensure the right things are built correctly
Write the full specification before delivery starts
quiz.why: Delivery analysis asks how each backlog item should be understood, elaborated and verified.

quiz.q: When does analysis happen at the Delivery Horizon?
opts: Continuously, just ahead of the work that needs it
quiz.why: Analysis is continuous and embedded in the iteration rhythm.

takeaways: Right things, built correctly.
Analysis is continuous and collaborative.
You'll leave with one item fully elaborated.

presenter.purpose: Set the frame for the day and choose a backlog item.
presenter.openingLine: "By five o'clock, one item from your backlog will be so clear that a developer, a tester and a customer would all describe it the same way."

beats.label: Welcome and outcomes
beats.notes: Leave-with artefacts; show the day map.

beats.label: Choose your item
beats.notes: Six minutes; chat waterfall of items.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Keep it brisk. Participants without a suitable item adopt the running case. Point out that the course follows chapter 7 of the book section by section.
presenter.whatGood: Every participant has an item, a user and a value statement.
presenter.commonFailure: Choosing an item that's really months of work — the fix: we'll decompose it in session 6; for now name it.
debrief: Whose item looks too big for one iteration?
What's the biggest unknown about yours?
presenter.answerKey: Running case: item = receiver delivery-window confirmation; serves receivers (and drivers indirectly); value = fewer failed first attempts, contributing to ≥92% on-time delivery.

modules.title: The Agile Business Analyst at this horizon
modules.subtitle: A full member of the team, not a gatekeeper

participant.bigIdea: At Delivery the analyst is a participant in delivery itself — not a gatekeeper between the business and the team.
participant.overview: For most Agile Business Analysts, the Delivery Horizon is where most working time is spent: closest to the customer, closest to the code, and closest to the moment of truth when an increment reaches users. The analyst is a **full member of the Agile Product Team**, working just ahead of the work that needs it, bringing depth of understanding and keeping a clear line of sight to the *why* behind each item.
objectives: Describe what the Agile BA does at the Delivery Horizon.
Explain the analyst's relationship with the Product Owner, Delivery Team and Iteration Manager.
Identify the analyst's role as a bridge to stakeholders.

keyPoints.title: Full team member
keyPoints.body: Attends planning and refinement, writes and refines stories, defines acceptance criteria, works with developers and testers, joins reviews.

keyPoints.title: Depth of understanding
keyPoints.body: Everyone contributes analysis; the Agile BA brings sustained focus on the 'why'.

keyPoints.title: Bridge to stakeholders
keyPoints.body: With the Product Owner, translates needs into backlog items and feeds back what the team learned.

keyPoints.title: Recognise false clarity
keyPoints.body: Notice when apparent clarity is concealing genuine ambiguity.

sections.heading: What the Agile BA does
sections.body:
- Attends **iteration planning** and contributes to **backlog refinement**.
- Writes and refines **user stories** and defines **acceptance criteria**.
- Collaborates with **developers and testers** throughout the iteration.
- Participates in **iteration reviews**.
- Keeps a line of sight from each item to the user need and the value it should create — so the team avoids solving the wrong problem even when requirements are technically correct.

sections.heading: The Agile Product Team
sections.body:
| Role | Focus | The Agile BA's relationship |
|---|---|---|
| Product Owner | *What* the team builds; voice of the customer; owns prioritisation | Supports by elaborating, documenting and facilitating; surfaces analysis that informs priority calls |
| Delivery Team | *How* it builds — developers, testers and others | Works alongside as a member; builds shared understanding |
| Iteration Manager | *How the team works together* (Scrum Master in Scrum) | Partners on effective events and continuous improvement |

Analysis is a **shared capability**: everyone asks questions and challenges assumptions. The dedicated analyst adds depth and continuity.

sections.heading: The bridge to stakeholders
sections.body:
Many stakeholders sit outside the team: in the running case, depot route planners, the WHS lead, Legal, the contact centre and key shippers. With the Product Owner, the Agile BA elicits and clarifies needs, turns them into backlog items, and reports back what the team learned and delivered.

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

activities.title: Where I add value
activities.instructions: For your item, list who you'll need to talk to, what each needs from you, and one place where 'apparent clarity' might be hiding ambiguity.

prompts.label: People and roles I'll work with on this item
Where apparent clarity might be hiding ambiguity

participant.aiPrompt: Act as an experienced agile business analyst. For the backlog item below, list the roles inside and outside the team I should involve, what each needs from me, and five questions that would expose ambiguity hiding behind apparently clear requirements. Item:

quiz.q: Who owns prioritisation of the product backlog?
quiz.why: The Agile BA informs priority calls; the Product Owner makes them.

quiz.q: The Agile BA's distinctive contribution at Delivery is…
opts: Being the only person who does analysis
Sustained focus on the 'why' behind each item
quiz.why: Analysis is shared; the dedicated analyst brings depth and context.

takeaways: Participant, not gatekeeper.
Hold the 'why' for the team.
Bridge to stakeholders, with the Product Owner.

presenter.purpose: Define the analyst's role and relationships at Delivery.
presenter.openingLine: "Who here has been described as 'the person between the business and IT'? Today we retire that description."

beats.label: The three roles
beats.notes: Product Owner, Delivery Team, Iteration Manager; analysis as a shared capability.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Use the book's framework-neutral terms (Iteration Manager, iteration). If participants use Scrum terms, map them and move on.
presenter.whatGood: A specific stakeholder list with needs, and one concrete ambiguity.
presenter.commonFailure: Positioning the BA as owner of priorities — the fix: the BA informs; the Product Owner decides.
debrief: Where does your team expect you to be a gatekeeper?
presenter.answerKey: Running case ambiguity: 'confirm delivery window' — does a confirmation lock the window, or can the receiver change it after route lock? Stakeholders: route planner (timing), WHS lead (safe-drop limits), Legal (SMS content and consent), contact centre (expired links).

modules.title: Outcomes of analysis
modules.subtitle: Five outcomes that let the team build the right thing

participant.bigIdea: Delivery analysis produces understanding, not documents — and it shows up in five outcomes.
participant.overview:
Analysis at this horizon produces outputs that let the team build the right thing, with shared understanding, within the time available — shaped by **team capacity** and **velocity**. These outputs emerge through collaboration and are refined as the work progresses.

![Five outcomes of Delivery Horizon analysis](/visuals/horizons-delivery/outcomes.svg)
objectives: Describe the five outcomes of analysis at the Delivery Horizon.
Recognise a well-elaborated backlog item and a well-prepared backlog.
Explain how validation and value-focus happen during the iteration.

keyPoints.title: Well-elaborated items
keyPoints.body: Small enough for an iteration, clear enough to start, testable enough to verify.

keyPoints.title: Well-prepared backlog
keyPoints.body: Decomposed, elaborated and ordered — continuously, not as an event.

keyPoints.title: Shared understanding
keyPoints.body: Invisible when present, expensive when absent.

keyPoints.title: Validated increments
keyPoints.body: Potentially releasable, verified against acceptance criteria.

keyPoints.title: Vision, customer, value
keyPoints.body: Counteract the gravitational pull of detail.

sections.heading: 7.3.1 Well-elaborated backlog items
sections.body: The team shares a picture of **the user, the context, the behaviour** and **how success will be judged**. Acceptance criteria are integral, not added afterwards: they cover typical and edge cases and are best derived from concrete examples. The item also carries everything learned in discussion — clarifications, constraints, testability concerns — and, where useful, **diagrams, models, prototypes, wireframes or process flows**.

sections.heading: 7.3.2 Well-prepared product backlog
sections.body:
**Decomposition, elaboration and prioritisation** are the main tools. Items for the next one or two iterations are ready to estimate and start; items further out need only be understood well enough to order and roughly size.

![Backlog readiness by distance from delivery](/visuals/horizons-delivery/backlog-readiness.svg)

sections.heading: 7.3.3 Shared understanding and 7.3.4 validated increments
sections.body: Much shared-understanding work is quiet: the conversation that prevents a misunderstanding, the edge case resolved before it's a defect. Each iteration ends with an increment that is **functionally complete, tested and verified against its acceptance criteria** — but validation is continuous, not a gate at the end. The analyst watches emerging work and raises deviations early.

sections.heading: 7.3.5 Focus on product vision, customer and value
sections.body: Detail has a gravitational pull. The analyst keeps the team connected to the vision (which of two equivalent implementations better serves the customer?), the customer (criteria written as user outcomes) and value (is this the most valuable work, and is it landing with users?).

activities.title: Outcome check
activities.instructions: Rate your item against the five outcomes (red / amber / green) and write the single action that would most improve the weakest one.

prompts.label: 7.3.5 Vision, customer and value — rating and why
Weakest outcome and my next action

activities.title: What belongs on the item
activities.instructions: List what you'd capture on your backlog item beyond the story statement: clarifications, constraints, and any diagram, model, prototype or process flow that would cut ambiguity.

participant.aiPrompt: Review the backlog item below against five outcomes of delivery analysis: (1) well-elaborated — user, context, behaviour, testable acceptance criteria covering edge cases; (2) fits a well-prepared backlog — small enough for one iteration, dependencies known; (3) shared understanding — open questions; (4) validation — how we'll verify it; (5) connection to the product vision, customer and value. Rate each red/amber/green with reasons and suggest one supporting artefact (diagram, wireframe, process flow) that would reduce ambiguity. Item:

quiz.q: Acceptance criteria are best treated as…
opts: A separate artefact added after the story
An integral part of a well-elaborated item
quiz.why: The book treats acceptance criteria as integral, ideally derived from examples.

quiz.q: How far should items 'much later' in the backlog be elaborated?
opts: Only enough to order and roughly size
To the same level as the current iteration
quiz.why: Over-elaborating items that may change or never be built is waste.

quiz.q: Validation at the Delivery Horizon is…
opts: A gate at the end of the iteration
A continuous activity throughout the iteration
quiz.why: The analyst monitors emerging work and raises deviations early.

takeaways: Five outcomes, not five documents.
Elaborate near-term items; order and size the rest.
Keep detail anchored to vision, customer and value.

presenter.purpose: Teach the five outcomes and diagnose participants' items.
presenter.openingLine: "If I asked your team what 'ready' means for the next story, would you all give the same answer?"

beats.label: Well-elaborated items and backlog readiness
beats.notes: Backlog readiness diagram; just in time.

beats.label: Activity: what belongs on the item
Debrief
beats.notes: Which outcome is weakest across the room?

presenter.facilitationNotes: Expect 7.3.5 to be the weakest for most people. Point to session 5 for 'think as a customer' and session 6 for decomposition.
presenter.whatGood: Honest ratings with a concrete next action; a supporting artefact that genuinely reduces ambiguity.
presenter.commonFailure: Rating everything green — the fix: ask 'could a tester write tests from it today?'
debrief: Which outcome is weakest in your team?
What artefact would save your team the most rework?
presenter.answerKey: Running case: 7.3.1 amber (criteria not agreed); 7.3.2 red (feature too big — needs decomposition); 7.3.3 amber (route-lock rule unclear); 7.3.4 amber (no plan to verify the run-sheet update); 7.3.5 green (clear link to on-time delivery). Supporting artefact: a state diagram for the consignment (notified → confirmed / safe drop / no response → route locked).

modules.title: Time frame · context, feedback and learning
modules.subtitle: Just in time, and the engine of agile delivery

participant.bigIdea: Elaborate close to delivery, and treat every iteration's feedback as the engine of learning.
participant.overview: The Delivery Horizon has the shortest time frame: a **one-to-four-week iteration**, or continuous flow in Kanban. Analysis is spread across the whole time box. It also produces the most frequent and concrete feedback: without it, iteration is merely repetition.
objectives: Describe the Delivery time frame for iterative and flow-based teams.
Apply just-in-time elaboration.
Identify the sources of feedback at Delivery and turn them into action.

keyPoints.title: Shortest time frame
keyPoints.body: 1–4 week iterations, or continuous flow.

keyPoints.title: Just in time
keyPoints.body: Requirements specified too early go stale; elaborate close to delivery.

keyPoints.title: Context shapes everything
keyPoints.body: The product vision, iteration goal and ordered backlog give each item meaning.

keyPoints.title: Feedback is the engine
keyPoints.body: Questions, refinement, reviews and retrospectives all surface learning.

sections.heading: 7.4 Time frame
sections.body:
| | Iteration-based | Flow-based (e.g. Kanban) |
|---|---|---|
| Cycle | 1–4 week iteration | Items move as capacity allows |
| Current work | Elaborated just before or just after it's picked up | Elaborated as it reaches the top of the queue |
| Future work | Refined enough for confident planning | Refined enough to keep the queue flowing |

Requirements specified far in advance go stale: priorities shift, users give feedback, constraints emerge. Elaborating close to delivery uses the most current understanding and reduces waste.

sections.heading: 7.5 Context, feedback and learning
sections.body:
**Context** — the product vision, the iteration goal, the ordered backlog and the understanding of user needs — gives each story its meaning. When context is unclear, the team makes assumptions, and assumptions are a primary source of rework.

![Feedback sources at the Delivery Horizon](/visuals/horizons-delivery/feedback-loops.svg)

The analyst listens for signals — questions that reveal misunderstandings, defects that point to unclear requirements, stories that fall short of expectations — and uses them to improve the next items. When a pattern appears (a feature is far more complex than expected, users aren't engaging), it goes to the Product Owner because it may change what's built next.

activities.title: Signals and actions
activities.instructions: List three recent feedback signals from your team (a question, a defect, a review reaction). For each, name what it reveals and the action it should trigger.

prompts.label: Context my team is missing (vision, iteration goal, user needs)

participant.aiPrompt: I'm an agile business analyst. Below are feedback signals from my team's last iterations (questions, defects, review reactions, retrospective notes). Group them into patterns, explain what each pattern reveals about our requirements or analysis process, and propose concrete changes to how we elaborate the next backlog items. Flag any pattern the Product Owner should hear about. Signals:

quiz.q: Why elaborate close to delivery?
opts: Requirements specified far in advance risk becoming obsolete
quiz.why: Priorities, feedback and constraints change; early detail is often discarded.

quiz.q: A defect that traces to an unclear requirement is best treated as…
opts: A signal to improve how following items are elaborated
A reason to write longer specifications
quiz.why: The analyst turns signals into better backlog items.

quiz.q: What gives an individual story its meaning?
opts: The context: product vision, iteration goal, ordered backlog and user needs
quiz.why: Without context the team makes assumptions — a major source of rework.

takeaways: Elaborate just in time.
Hold the context consciously.
Feedback is information — act on it.

presenter.purpose: Teach the time frame and the feedback discipline.
presenter.openingLine: "How old is the oldest fully specified story in your backlog? What's the chance it's still right?"

beats.label: Time frame: iteration vs flow
beats.notes: Poll: who works in iterations, who in flow?

beats.label: Context
beats.notes: What happens when context is missing.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Pre-lunch: keep the teach short and the activity concrete. Expect many to say their team lacks a clear iteration goal — note it for session 8.
presenter.whatGood: Specific signals linked to specific changes in elaboration practice.
presenter.commonFailure: Generic actions ('communicate better') — the fix: what will you do differently on the next item?
debrief: What signal does your team most often ignore?
Who needs to hear your pattern?
presenter.answerKey: Running case signals: developers asked twice whether an expired link should reveal consignment details (→ privacy rule unclear; add explicit criterion); review showed drivers ignoring safe-drop notes on the run sheet (→ usability issue; involve drivers in refinement); confirmations lower on Mondays (→ pattern for the Product Owner).

modules.title: Applying the nine principles
modules.subtitle: Habits of thinking, most visible in day-to-day delivery

participant.bigIdea: The nine principles aren't a checklist — at Delivery they're habits you can see in every conversation.
participant.overview:
The book's nine principles of agile business analysis — remembered as **STAG US Pursue, Avoid and Embrace** — shape how the analyst works. At the Delivery Horizon, where work is concrete and fast-moving, they're most visible in practice.

![The nine principles of agile business analysis](/visuals/horizons-delivery/principles.svg)
objectives: Name the nine principles in order.
Describe how each shows up at the Delivery Horizon.
Apply three principles to your own backlog item.

keyPoints.title: Get Real Using Examples
keyPoints.body: Perhaps the most practically powerful principle at Delivery.

keyPoints.title: Avoid Waste
keyPoints.body: Just in time, not just in case.

keyPoints.title: Embrace Uncertainty and Change
keyPoints.body: Misunderstandings and surprises are information.

sections.heading: The principles at Delivery
sections.body:
| Principle | At the Delivery Horizon | Running case |
|---|---|---|
| **S** See the Whole | Keep the story → iteration goal → product outcome in view while working on detail | The confirmation only matters if the driver's run sheet updates |
| **T** Think as a Customer | Write criteria from the user's perspective; bring stories to life with examples | What does a receiver see at 6 am, after route lock? |
| **A** Analyze to Determine What is Valuable | Focus elaboration on the parts carrying the most risk or uncertainty | Route-lock timing and safe-drop rules, not button colours |
| **G** Get Real Using Examples | Replace abstract statements with concrete examples | House / apartment with concierge / closed small business |
| **U** Understand What is Feasible | Find the simplest implementation that satisfies the need; avoid gold-plating | SMS first; email fallback later |
| **S** Stimulate Collaboration | Come to events with examples and questions; make sure everyone is heard | Route planner and tester in refinement |
| **P** Pursue Continuous Improvement | Ask in the retro whether analysis is serving the team | Are criteria consistently testable? |
| **A** Avoid Waste | Just in time, not just in case; criteria sufficient, not exhaustive | Defer email-fallback wording |
| **E** Embrace Uncertainty and Change | Treat surprises as information, not failure | Low Monday confirmations → learn why |

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.heading: From abstract to concrete
sections.body:
*Abstract:* 'The system shall allow receivers to choose a safe drop.'

*Concrete:* 'When a receiver at a house selects **Front porch**, the instruction appears on the driver's run sheet; items over 25 kg are not offered a safe drop, and the receiver is told why.'

The second version leaves far less room for misinterpretation and gives developers and testers an unambiguous target.

activities.title: Three principles on my item
activities.instructions: Pick the three principles most at risk for your backlog item. For each, write what applying it would look like this iteration.

prompts.label: Principle 1 — what applying it looks like
Principle 2 — what applying it looks like
Principle 3 — what applying it looks like
One abstract statement rewritten as a concrete example

participant.aiPrompt: Act as an agile business analysis coach. For the backlog item below, apply each of the nine principles of agile business analysis (See the Whole; Think as a Customer; Analyze to Determine What is Valuable; Get Real Using Examples; Understand What is Feasible; Stimulate Collaboration; Pursue Continuous Improvement; Avoid Waste; Embrace Uncertainty and Change) and tell me, for each, one specific thing I should do this iteration. Then rewrite any abstract requirement as a concrete example. Item:

quiz.q: What does the mnemonic 'STAG US Pursue, Avoid and Embrace' help you remember?
quiz.why: Each letter is a principle, in the book's order.

quiz.q: 'Understand What is Feasible' at Delivery means…
opts: Reducing quality to fit the iteration
Finding the simplest implementation that genuinely satisfies the need
quiz.why: It keeps work moving and prevents gold-plating — not a licence to cut quality.

quiz.q: Which is the best expression of 'Avoid Waste' at Delivery?
opts: Elaborate only what is needed, when it is needed
quiz.why: Just in time, not just in case.

takeaways: Nine principles, STAG US Pursue, Avoid and Embrace.
Reach for examples whenever a requirement feels abstract.
Surprises are information.

presenter.purpose: Make the nine principles concrete at Delivery.
presenter.openingLine: "Which of these nine would your developers say you already live — and which would they say you don't?"

beats.label: Walk the table
beats.notes: Two or three rows in depth; ask for examples from the room.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Post-lunch energy: use a quick poll on 'which principle is hardest'. Be precise that the book has nine principles, including Pursue Continuous Improvement and Embrace Uncertainty and Change as separate principles.

roleplay.line: "I got a text at 9 pm asking if I'll be home tomorrow — I'm on night shift, so what do I pick?"
roleplay.curveball: "And is this text even real? It's got a link."
roleplay.move: Think as a Customer: capture 'night-shift receiver' as a new example and the trust concern as a criterion (sender name, retailer and consignment reference, no login or payment requested).

presenter.whatGood: Three principles applied with specific actions; a genuinely concrete example.
presenter.commonFailure: Restating the principle as the action ('I'll see the whole') — the fix: what will you check, with whom, this week?
debrief: Which principle is hardest in your team?
What did the roleplay add to the examples?
presenter.answerKey: Running case: Get Real — agree four receiver examples with the route planner; Avoid Waste — defer email fallback; Embrace Uncertainty — treat low Monday confirmation rates as a question to investigate.

modules.title: Analysis techniques: stories and elaboration
modules.subtitle: User stories, job stories, story decomposition and elaboration, NFRs, metrics and KPIs

participant.bigIdea: Thin, valuable slices with concrete examples are the analyst's highest-leverage Delivery technique.
participant.overview: Section 7.7.1 lists the analysis techniques commonly applied at the Delivery Horizon. This session covers the ones you'll use on every item: **User Stories**, **Job Stories**, **Story Decomposition**, **Story Elaboration**, **Non-Functional Requirements** and **Metrics and KPIs**. Session 7 covers the rest.
objectives: Express a backlog item as a user story or a job story.
Decompose a feature into independently valuable stories.
Elaborate a story with examples, acceptance criteria and NFRs.
Anchor a story to a measurable indicator.

keyPoints.title: User Stories
keyPoints.body: As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit].

keyPoints.title: Job Stories
keyPoints.body: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].

keyPoints.title: Decompose by value
keyPoints.body: Each slice independently valuable, testable and demonstrable.

keyPoints.title: Elaborate
keyPoints.body: User, context, goal, behaviour and acceptance criteria — the central Delivery activity.

keyPoints.title: NFRs and metrics
keyPoints.body: In criteria or the definition of done; measurable indicators at story level.

sections.heading: User Stories and Job Stories
sections.body:
**User story:** *As a receiver, I want to confirm my delivery window or choose a safe drop from the notification, so that my consignment arrives on the first attempt.*

**Job story:** *When I get a delivery notice the evening before and I'll be at work, I want to tell the driver where to leave it safely, so I can get my parcel without rearranging my day.*

Job stories help when the **situation and motivation** drive behaviour more than the user's role does.

sections.heading: Story Decomposition
sections.body:
![Splitting by value versus by layer](/visuals/horizons-delivery/decomposition.svg)

Feature: **receiver delivery-window confirmation**. Value slices:

1. Notify receiver by SMS the evening before (happy path).
2. Receiver confirms the window or chooses a safe drop via a one-click link.
3. Notify by email when no mobile number is on file.
4. Flag to the depot when a receiver hasn't responded by route lock.
5. Handle consignments with no receiver contact details.

Splitting along technical lines creates dependencies and many 'done' stories with nothing to show users.

sections.heading: Story Elaboration
sections.body:
![From examples to acceptance criteria](/visuals/horizons-delivery/examples-to-criteria.svg)

| Example | Receiver | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | House, at home | One-click confirm; driver run updated |
| 2 | House, at work | Chooses 'front porch'; instruction on run sheet |
| 3 | Small business | Confirms without creating an account |
| 4 | Link opened after 5 am route lock | Expiry message and contact details; no consignment data shown |

- *Given* a notified receiver, *when* they select Confirm, *then* the consignment is marked 'receiver confirmed' and the driver's run updates within 5 minutes.
- *Given* the receiver chooses a safe drop, *when* they submit, *then* the instruction appears on the driver's run sheet.
- *Given* a link opened after route lock, *when* it loads, *then* the receiver sees an expiry message and no consignment data.

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.heading: Non-Functional Requirements, Metrics and KPIs
sections.body:
| NFR | Story-level requirement (illustrative) |
|---|---|
| Privacy | Receiver sees only their own consignment; driver sees only address and safe-drop instruction |
| Security | Single-use, time-limited link; no login or payment requested |
| Accessibility | Meets WCAG 2.2 AA; works on mobile |
| Performance | Page loads in under 2 seconds on 4G |
| Safety | Safe drop never requires climbing, entering premises or lifting over a fence; items over 25 kg not offered |
| Audit | Every confirmation logged with timestamp and source |

NFRs go in explicit acceptance criteria or the definition of done, so they aren't deferred indefinitely.

**Story-level indicator:** % of notified receivers who confirm or choose a safe drop within 4 hours — anchored to the product's measure of fewer failed first attempts.

activities.title: Decompose
activities.instructions: Split your item into at least four independently valuable stories. Mark the first to elaborate and why.

activities.title: Elaborate one story
activities.instructions: For your first story write: the user or job story, four or more examples (including an unhappy path), three Given/When/Then criteria, relevant NFRs and a measurable indicator. You'll finish it in session 9.

participant.aiPrompt: Act as an agile business analyst. For the feature below: (1) decompose it into four to six independently valuable stories (not technical layers); (2) for the first story, write it as a user story and as a job story; (3) propose at least five concrete examples including edge cases and an unhappy path; (4) derive three to five Given/When/Then acceptance criteria from the examples; (5) list NFRs (privacy, security, accessibility, performance, audit, safety) and a measurable indicator of success. Flag ambiguities for the Product Owner. Feature:

quiz.q: Which is a value-based way to decompose a story?
opts: By business rule, data variation or happy/unhappy path
quiz.why: Each slice must be independently valuable and testable.

quiz.q: A job story frames a requirement in terms of…
quiz.why: That's what distinguishes it from a user story.

quiz.q: Where should NFRs live so they aren't deferred?
opts: In a separate document for later
In explicit acceptance criteria or the definition of done
quiz.why: Section 7.7.1: represent them in criteria or the definition of done.

takeaways: Decompose by value.
Examples first, criteria second.
NFRs and metrics belong on the item.

presenter.purpose: Produce the main leave-with artefact: one story decomposed and elaborated.
presenter.openingLine: "Let's take one small slice and make it so clear that nobody could build the wrong thing."

beats.label: Activity: elaborate
beats.notes: Pairs or trios; visit rooms at 10 and 20 minutes.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Groups write criteria before examples — redirect. Insist on one unhappy path and one privacy NFR. Unfinished work is fine: session 9 completes it.
presenter.whatGood: Value slices; four or more examples incl. an unhappy path; criteria traceable to examples; NFRs; a measurable indicator.
presenter.commonFailure: Criteria that restate the story — the fix: what exact observable result, for which example?
debrief: Which NFR would you normally miss?
presenter.answerKey: Model slices and elaboration as in the sections. Extra examples: apartment with concierge; consignment split across two days; 30 kg safe-drop request (rejected); duplicate notification for the same consignment.

modules.title: Analysis techniques: understanding and uncertainty
modules.subtitle: Keeping the user in view, resolving ambiguity, and deciding at the right moment

participant.bigIdea: Pick the technique that resolves the specific ambiguity in front of you — not the one you always use.
participant.overview: The remaining analysis techniques from section 7.7.1 fall into three jobs: **keeping the user in view**, **resolving ambiguity and complexity**, and **managing uncertainty and scope**. Each is a precision tool, not overhead.
objectives: Describe each remaining Delivery analysis technique and when to use it.
Match a technique to a specific ambiguity.
Plan a spike or real-options decision for your item.

keyPoints.title: Keep the user in view
keyPoints.body: Personas, Customer Journey Maps, Story Mapping, Storyboarding, Prototyping.

keyPoints.title: Resolve ambiguity
keyPoints.body: Discovery Workshops, Event Storming, Stakeholder Analysis, Problem Definition.

keyPoints.title: Manage uncertainty
keyPoints.body: Spikes, Real Options, MVP, Root Cause Analysis.

sections.heading: The toolkit
sections.body:
| Technique | Use it at Delivery when… |
|---|---|
| **Personas** | The team is deep in detail and needs the user's goals and context in view |
| **Customer Journey Maps** | Optimising one story risks creating friction elsewhere in the user's experience |
| **Story Mapping** | You need to see where the item sits in the user journey and what can be deferred (maintain the existing map; don't build a new one) |
| **Storyboarding** | You need to walk stakeholders through an interaction flow |
| **Prototyping, Mock-ups and Wireframes** | A rough visual would resolve an ambiguity faster than words |
| **Discovery Workshops** | A complex or contested requirement can't be resolved in informal conversation |
| **Event Storming** | Complex domain behaviour needs modelling (events, commands, aggregates) |
| **Spikes** | Uncertainty blocks elaboration or estimation — time-box an investigation |
| **Real Options** | You can defer a decision to the last responsible moment |
| **Minimum Viable Product** | Scoping the simplest implementation that delivers value |
| **Problem Definition and Analysis** | A requirement is drifting from the original problem |
| **Root Cause Analysis** | Recurring defects or missed outcomes signal a systemic issue |
| **Stakeholder Analysis** | You need to know who to consult, who accepts, and who is affected |

sections.heading: Running case: choosing the technique
sections.body:
| Ambiguity | Technique |
|---|---|
| What may the SMS contain, and what consent is needed? | **Spike** with Legal, time-boxed to two days |
| Drivers ignore safe-drop notes on the run sheet | **Prototyping** a revised run-sheet line with three drivers |
| Should a confirmation lock the window or allow changes until route lock? | **Real Options** — decide when the route-lock integration is understood |
| Where does confirmation sit relative to tracking and redelivery? | **Story Mapping** — check the existing map |
| Failed first attempts rising at one depot despite confirmations | **Root Cause Analysis**, findings to the Product Owner |

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

activities.title: Match the technique
activities.instructions: List the two or three biggest ambiguities or uncertainties on your item. For each, choose a technique from the toolkit, say why, and what you'd do first.

prompts.label: A decision I can defer (real options) and until when

participant.aiPrompt: I'm an agile business analyst. For each ambiguity or uncertainty on my backlog item below, recommend the most suitable technique from: Personas, Customer Journey Maps, Story Mapping, Storyboarding, Prototyping/Mock-ups/Wireframes, Discovery Workshops, Event Storming, Spikes, Real Options, Minimum Viable Product, Problem Definition and Analysis, Root Cause Analysis, Stakeholder Analysis. Explain why, and give a concrete first step and time-box. Item and ambiguities:

quiz.q: A spike is…
opts: A time-boxed investigation to resolve uncertainty blocking elaboration or estimation
quiz.why: It explores the question without committing to full delivery.

quiz.q: At the Delivery Horizon, Story Mapping means…
opts: Building a new map for each iteration
Referencing and maintaining the existing map
quiz.why: Delivery maintains the map and feeds observations back.

quiz.q: Real options thinking helps the analyst…
opts: Defer decisions to the last responsible moment
quiz.why: It avoids committing before the team understands enough to choose well.

takeaways: Name the ambiguity, then pick the tool.
Spikes and real options tame uncertainty.
Keep the user visible with personas, journeys and prototypes.

presenter.purpose: Cover the remaining analysis techniques and match them to real ambiguities.
presenter.openingLine: "What's the one question on your item that nobody in the team can answer yet?"

beats.label: Three jobs and the toolkit
beats.notes: Walk the table by job, not alphabetically.

beats.label: Activity
beats.notes: Individual, then pair to challenge choices.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Don't try to teach every technique in depth — the full descriptions are in the book's technique chapters. Focus on choosing the right one.
presenter.whatGood: Each ambiguity matched to a technique with a concrete, time-boxed first step.
presenter.commonFailure: Defaulting to 'a workshop' for everything — the fix: would a two-hour spike or a rough sketch resolve it faster?
debrief: Which technique was new to you?
presenter.answerKey: As in the running-case table. Real option: whether confirmation locks the window — defer until the route-lock integration spike reports.

modules.title: Planning and delivery techniques
modules.subtitle: Three Amigos, Planning Workshops, Relative Estimation, Collaborative Games, the Kanban Board and the Product Roadmap

participant.bigIdea: The best planning techniques are structured conversations that surface misunderstanding early.
participant.overview:
Section 7.7.2 names six planning and delivery techniques for the Delivery Horizon. Each one turns a team event into a chance to build shared understanding — the Three Amigos above all.

![The Three Amigos](/visuals/horizons-delivery/three-amigos.svg)
objectives: Run a Three Amigos conversation on a backlog item.
Prepare items for a Planning Workshop and contribute to Relative Estimation.
Use Collaborative Games, the Kanban Board and the Product Roadmap at Delivery.

keyPoints.title: Three Amigos
keyPoints.body: Analyst, developer and tester mindsets on one item before the team commits.

keyPoints.title: Planning Workshops
keyPoints.body: Iteration planning: items elaborated, criteria clear, risks known.

keyPoints.title: Relative Estimation
keyPoints.body: Hard to estimate usually means not yet elaborated.

keyPoints.title: Collaborative Games
keyPoints.body: E.g. Planning Poker — surface hidden differences in understanding.

keyPoints.title: Kanban Board
keyPoints.body: A story stuck for days often signals an unresolved ambiguity.

keyPoints.title: Product Roadmap
keyPoints.body: Context for where this iteration fits; delivery learning can revise it.

sections.heading: The six techniques
sections.body:
| Technique | The Agile BA's contribution |
|---|---|
| **Three Amigos** | Brings the analyst mindset; facilitates; captures examples and criteria |
| **Planning Workshops** | Prepares items so the team can estimate and commit; resolves elaboration questions during the session |
| **Relative Estimation** | Makes sure items are understood well enough to estimate; surfaces hidden complexity |
| **Collaborative Games** | Uses games such as Planning Poker to make differences in understanding visible |
| **Kanban Board** | Monitors flow; spots items blocked by analysis questions |
| **Product Roadmap** | Uses it as context; feeds back when delivery learning should change it |

sections.heading: Running a Three Amigos session
sections.body:
1. **Pick one item** due in the next iteration.
2. **Bring 3–5 people** covering the analyst, developer and tester mindsets.
3. **Start from examples**: walk the happy path, then ask 'what could go wrong?'
4. **Capture** agreed examples, new questions and acceptance criteria on the item.
5. **Stop** when the team can estimate and start — not when every scenario is written.

The output is shared understanding plus examples and criteria — not a document.

sections.heading: Where the techniques live in agile events
sections.body:
| Event | Techniques in play |
|---|---|
| Backlog refinement | Three Amigos, Story Elaboration, Relative Estimation |
| Iteration planning | Planning Workshop, Relative Estimation, Collaborative Games |
| Daily standup | Kanban Board — spot items stuck on questions |
| Iteration review | Validate the increment; capture feedback as backlog items |
| Retrospective | Pursue Continuous Improvement in the analysis process |

activities.title: Three Amigos roleplay
activities.instructions: In trios (analyst, developer, tester), run a 12-minute Three Amigos on one participant's story. Swap roles if time allows. Capture what changed.

prompts.label: Would we estimate it now? Why / why not?

activities.title: Planning readiness
activities.instructions: Is your story ready for a Planning Workshop? Note what's still needed and which collaborative game you'd use in estimation.

participant.aiPrompt: Play the developer and tester in a Three Amigos conversation about the backlog item below. As the developer, ask how it could be built and what's technically unclear. As the tester, ask what could go wrong, including edge cases and unhappy paths. Ask one question at a time and wait for my answer; after ten exchanges, summarise the agreed examples, open questions and acceptance criteria. Item:

quiz.q: Who takes part in a Three Amigos conversation?
opts: People representing the analyst, developer and tester mindsets
quiz.why: Three to five people bringing the three mindsets.

quiz.q: An item is very hard to estimate. That most likely signals…
opts: The item hasn't been adequately elaborated
The PO should decide the estimate
quiz.why: A signal for more analysis, not a reason to proceed.

quiz.q: A story has sat 'in progress' on the Kanban Board for days. The analyst should…
opts: Check for an unresolved ambiguity they can help address
Move it back to the backlog
quiz.why: Stuck items often signal analysis questions.

takeaways: Three Amigos before commitment.
Hard to estimate = not yet elaborated.
Use the board to spot stuck questions.

presenter.purpose: Practise the Three Amigos and connect the six techniques to team events.
presenter.openingLine: "Fifteen minutes of three people arguing about examples saves days of rework. Let's prove it."

beats.label: Events table and debrief
beats.notes: Where do these live in your team?

presenter.facilitationNotes: Assign trio roles explicitly; give testers licence to be awkward. Keep event language framework-neutral.

roleplay.persona: Dev, a developer in the trio
roleplay.line: "What happens if the receiver confirms, then the retailer splits the order into two consignments?"
roleplay.curveball: "And the run sheet is generated by a vendor system — we can't change its layout this iteration."
roleplay.move: Capture the split-consignment case as a new example and probably a new story; treat the vendor constraint with Understand What is Feasible — show the instruction in the existing notes field for now.

presenter.whatGood: New examples and questions surfaced, criteria changed, a clear call on estimability.
presenter.commonFailure: The analyst presenting the story rather than discussing it — the fix: open with an example and a question.
debrief: What did the tester find that you'd missed?
presenter.answerKey: Typical Three Amigos additions in the running case: split consignments; receiver changes mind after confirming; link forwarded to someone else; vendor run-sheet constraint.

modules.title: Exercise: elaborate one backlog item · close
modules.subtitle: Finish your item, check it against the outcomes, commit

participant.bigIdea: One item, fully understood, beats a hundred specified ones.
participant.overview: Finalise the item you've been building all day: story, examples, criteria, NFRs and a measurable indicator, plus anything the Three Amigos surfaced. Check it against the five outcomes, then commit to what you'll do differently next iteration.
objectives: Finalise one fully elaborated backlog item.
Check it against the five outcomes of analysis.
Commit to one change in your delivery practice.

keyPoints.title: Complete the item
keyPoints.body: Story, examples, criteria, NFRs, indicator, supporting artefacts.

keyPoints.title: Check it
keyPoints.body: Against the five outcomes.

keyPoints.title: Commit
keyPoints.body: One technique and one principle you'll apply next iteration.

sections.heading: Exercise brief
sections.body:
1. Finalise your story with everything learned today.
2. Check it against the five outcomes (7.3.1–7.3.5).
3. Name one technique and one principle you'll apply next iteration.

sections.heading: The finished running-case item
sections.body:
| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| Story | Receiver confirms window or chooses a safe drop via one-click link |
| Examples | House at home; house at work → porch; small business; link after route lock; 30 kg safe drop rejected; split consignment |
| Criteria | Run updated within 5 min; safe drop on run sheet; expired link shows no data |
| NFRs | Privacy, security, WCAG 2.2 AA, < 2 s load, safety limits, audit log |
| Indicator | % confirming or choosing safe drop within 4 hours |
| Artefacts | Consignment state diagram; run-sheet line prototype |

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

prompts.label: Final story with examples, criteria and NFRs
Commitment: a technique I'll apply next iteration
Commitment: a principle I'll practise next iteration

participant.aiPrompt: Review my elaborated backlog item below as a peer agile business analyst. Check: examples include edge and unhappy cases; acceptance criteria derive from the examples and are observable; NFRs are explicit; there is a measurable indicator; it is small enough for one iteration; and it is connected to the product vision, customer and value. List the three most important improvements. Item:

quiz.q: Which belongs in a fully elaborated item in this course?
opts: Detailed UI designs for every screen
Examples, criteria, NFRs and a measurable indicator
quiz.why: These are the elements built today.

quiz.q: The best final check of an item is…
quiz.why: The outcomes describe what good delivery analysis produces.

takeaways: You leave with one item fully elaborated.
Check items against the five outcomes.
Practise one technique and one principle next iteration.

presenter.purpose: Consolidate the artefact and secure commitments.
presenter.openingLine: "This morning it was a line on a backlog. Let's see what it is now."

beats.label: Individual work
beats.notes: Circulate; check criteria trace to examples.

beats.label: Commitments round
beats.notes: Everyone posts one commitment in chat.

presenter.facilitationNotes: End on time. Read the finished running-case table aloud as the final moment.
presenter.whatGood: A complete item and specific commitments.
presenter.commonFailure: Running out of time — the fix: prioritise the outcome check and commitments over polishing.
debrief: What's your commitment for next iteration?
presenter.answerKey: Model item as in the table. Outcome check: all five amber-to-green; remaining risk is the route-lock integration, covered by a spike.
